description: Somos un equipo con experiencia en desarrollo de software y sistemas. Nos gustan los retos y poner a prueba ideas fuera de la caja; en equipo disfrutamos de un buen ambiente y venimos a desarrollar una solución real. Estamos abiertos a recibir más integrantes, escríbannos, gracias!
summary: Trend Detective is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) web app that helps students and the public become Earth-data detectives. A user picks a place (search, map, coordinates or a ready-made example) and a plain question (heat, water or air, with seven finer sub-topics). The app shortlists NASA variables that can answer it (AIRS, GPM IMERG, OMI, GLDAS, and MERRA-2 via NASA POWER), fetches monthly time series from NASA Giovanni and NASA POWER, removes the seasonal cycle, and reports the rate of change per decade (Sen's slope) with a 95% range. Significance needs two tests to agree (Mann-Kendall with Hamed-Rao correction, and OLS with effective sample size), followed by robustness checks (leave one year out, known satellite drift, a second instrument) and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across variables. The result is an honest "how sure are we" verdict, shown in a Simple (kid-friendly, glossary-backed) or Scientific view. It matters because a variable can trend one way in one place and the opposite way in another: the tool shows what is changing, where, by how much, and whether it is significant, and says "too soon to tell" when the data cannot decide yet.
details:
1. Project description

1.1 What does it do?

Trend Detective (Earth System Trend Detective) helps high-school and college students and the public find out what is changing in a place, by how much, and whether the change is real, using NASA Earth-science data. A user answers a short series of questions (where, and what about: heat, water or air), sees which NASA variables can answer that question, and gets a multi-year chart with the seasonal cycle removed, the rate of change per 10 years with a 95% range, and a plain "how sure are we" verdict. Every result can be read in a Simple view (kid-friendly words backed by a glossary) or a Scientific view, in English or Spanish.

1.2 How does it work?

  • Pick a place: search by name, click on a map, type coordinates, or open a ready-made place (Cajamarca highlands in Peru, Wisconsin in the USA, and example points near Delhi, Manaus and Tamanrasset).
  • Pick a question: three main questions (heat, water, air) and seven sub-topics (hot afternoons, warm nights, rain, damp air, wet ground, smoke and haze, burning fuel).
  • Shortlist: a hand-written catalog of NASA variables, each with a simple definition, units, known data problems and the reason to look at it, shows which variables can answer the question for that place.
  • Get the data: monthly series come from the NASA Giovanni time-series service (AIRS, GPM IMERG, GLDAS, OMI, MERRA-2 aerosols) and NASA POWER (MERRA-2 temperature, rain and humidity). Pre-loaded places are saved as static files, so the demo does not depend on a live NASA service.
  • One fixed analysis protocol: remove the seasonal cycle, estimate the trend with Sen's slope and a 95% range, then two decisive tests that must agree (Mann-Kendall with the Hamed-Rao autocorrelation correction, and OLS with an effective sample size). Seasonal Mann-Kendall is shown for context. Robustness checks: leave one year out, known satellite drift years (AIRS on Aqua is cut at December 2021 because of orbit drift), and a "second opinion" from another instrument measuring the same quantity. When a whole question is scanned, Benjamini-Hochberg controls false discoveries. We also estimate how many years of data would be needed to detect a trend.
  • Verdict: a mechanical label (significant, significant but fragile, borderline, possibly changing, no detectable change, or can't tell), written in both registers.
  • Context: the place is located in its IPCC AR6 reference region, its climate type is estimated (Koppen-Geiger rules on NASA POWER climatology), and for the ready-made places the app shows what the IPCC AR6 report found for that region, kept visibly separate from our own result.
  • Share: a real change can be saved to a "detective notebook" kept only in the browser, and shared as a plain-text report or JSON file. Nothing is sent to a server.

1.3 Innovation and purpose

The challenge notes that the same process can push a variable up in one region and down in another, and that the large number of variables makes it hard to choose one. Our answer is to start from a plain question instead of a variable name, to apply the same declared protocol to every variable, and to be honest about uncertainty: the tool says "too soon to tell" when the record is too short, flags known instrument problems (satellite drift, the OMI row anomaly, model input changes), and never merges two instruments into one number. Guided "Watch a demo" walkthroughs show new users how the tool works.

1.4 Benefits and impact

A. Social, environmental and technological benefits: it turns open NASA data into something a student can explore and question; it teaches the difference between a change and a significant change; it is free, its code is public, it works in two languages and runs on a laptop or on a local network.

B. Contribution to the SDGs / space missions: it supports SDG 4 (Quality Education: data and statistical literacy) and SDG 13 (Climate Action: understanding local climate change from evidence). Its water and air questions touch topics of SDG 6 and SDG 11. It increases the use of data from NASA Earth-science missions (Aqua, Aura, GPM) and models (MERRA-2, GLDAS).

C. Expected impact in the community: our local event is in Cajamarca, Peru. We want students and teachers in our region (and anywhere) to check claims about their own place with real data, in Spanish, instead of relying only on global headlines.

1.5 Objectives and expected results

  • Identify Earth-science variables that can answer a plain question for a place.
  • Acquire the data for a chosen region or point.
  • Generate and visualize a long enough time series for statistical analysis.
  • Report the rate of change and test its significance (Mann-Kendall, t-test on the OLS slope with effective sample size, confidence intervals), as the challenge asks.

1.6 Methodology and work plan

The project was built during the hackathon weekend (14-15 November 2026) in released versions:

  • v0.1.0 (14 Nov): MVP: analysis engine, API and kid-friendly web app; live NASA POWER places; versioning, changelog and CI.
  • v2.0.0 (15 Nov): live NASA data for any place (Giovanni + POWER), second-opinion instrument check, IPCC context, Spanish interface.
  • v2.1.0 (15 Nov): area-weighted box means, honest Simple view, known data breaks, "How it works" page, sub-topics, new design.
  • Latest (15 Nov): detective notebook, report/JSON sharing, map fixes, AI-use disclosure on the Sources page.

Intermediate deliverables: Giovanni area-averaged CSV downloads for the first Cajamarca test box (AIRS relative humidity, day and night), monthly temperature (AIRS, MERRA-2/POWER), precipitation (GPM IMERG, MERRA-2/POWER), soil moisture and evaporation (GLDAS), haze and NO2 (OMI), precomputed results for the ready-made places, and a documented sources check (docs/sources-checked.md in the repo).

1.7 Methodology and tools

1.7.1 Tools and software: NASA Giovanni (time-series API and web export), NASA POWER API, NASA Earthdata login/token, GitHub and GitHub Actions (tests, build, releases), Docker (optional deployment).

1.7.2 Programming languages and frameworks: Python 3.12 (NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, Pydantic, FastAPI, Uvicorn, pytest, uv); TypeScript with React 19 and Vite, Plotly.js (charts), Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles (maps), Vitest. Data cards are written in YAML and the result format is a JSON Schema shared by backend and frontend.

1.7.3 Hardware and sensors: no hardware or sensors of our own. All measurements come from NASA satellite instruments (AIRS on Aqua, OMI on Aura, GPM IMERG multi-satellite rainfall) and NASA models (MERRA-2, GLDAS).

1.8 Project management

Team D.E.V.S.: Renato Leon (team owner), Jhan Marco Torres Edquen, Leonardo Mathias Perez Sanchez.

1.9 Location

Local event: Cajamarca, Peru. The tool works for any land point or box on Earth. Our main ready-made place is the Cajamarca highlands in the northern Peruvian Andes, because it is our home region and a mountain area where scientific findings are uncertain (IPCC AR6 gives low confidence for heavy rain and drought trends there), so it is a good place to show both clear changes and honest "can't tell yet" results. Wisconsin and the example points (Delhi, Manaus, Tamanrasset) show very different climates.

1.10 Impact and relevance to NASA's mission

It puts NASA Earth Science Division data (Giovanni, GES DISC, NASA POWER) in the hands of students and the public, follows open-science practice (public code, every number traceable to a named NASA dataset and our statistics code), and explains instrument limits openly.

1.11 Expected results

For any place, the user gets: what is changing, by how much per decade, and how sure we can be. Example from the app's saved results: for the Wisconsin box, MERRA-2 2 m air temperature (via NASA POWER) rises about 0.34 °C per decade (95% range 0.16 to 0.51), 1981-2025, and both tests agree it is significant. Many other results honestly come out as "no detectable change" or "can't tell here".

1.12 Conclusions and future improvements

Lessons learned: long satellite records need care (Aqua orbit drift, OMI row anomaly, GPM's TRMM-to-GPM change, model input changes in MERRA-2 and GLDAS); not every NASA variable is available through the Giovanni cloud API (MODIS aerosol and MOPITT CO are only manual exports for now); a box that mixes coast and mountains gives misleading averages, so we added a homogeneity check; a grid "point" covers a different area for each instrument.

Possible optimizations: server-side area averages for fine grids, MODIS and MOPITT when available, ground-station comparison (for example NOAA Climate Data Online), coupling checks between related variables (rain and soil water), a neighbouring-box check, and more ready-made places.

1.13 Annexes

Demo: https://rennleon.github.io/hackaton-nasa-space-apps-2026/ . Code, instructions to run it, changelog and the full reference list: https://github.com/rennleon/hackaton-nasa-space-apps-2026 (see docs/sources-checked.md). The app's Sources page lists every instrument, dataset and link.

2. Use of AI

The team used AI tools (Claude Code by Anthropic) to brainstorm, to help write and debug code, to write, edit and translate text (including this submission), to help research and check references (the sources check in docs/sources-checked.md was an AI-assisted pass, marked as needing human confirmation), and to help with visual design and the demo presentation. The app itself uses no AI: all numbers come from NASA data and our statistics code. This is also disclosed on the app's Sources page and in the README.

3. NASA data

NASA Giovanni and NASA POWER; AIRS L3 monthly V7.0 (AIRS3STM); GPM IMERG Final monthly V07; GLDAS Noah 2.1 monthly; OMI OMNO2d and OMAERUVd V003; MERRA-2 (via NASA POWER and Giovanni); CERES SYN1deg (via NASA POWER). Full links are in the NASA Data field.

4. Other data and references

IPCC AR6 WGI report and reference regions, Koppen-Geiger climate rules (Beck et al. 2018), Vuille and Bradley (2000), papers on the NASA datasets we use (Krotkov et al. 2016, Torres et al. 2018, Gelaro et al. 2017) and statistics method papers (Mann 1945, Sen 1968, Hamed and Rao 1998, Benjamini and Hochberg 1995, Weatherhead et al. 1998). Links are in the Space Agency Partner & Other Data field. Other sources and tools used to build the app (not NASA-related): NOAA/NCICS State Climate Summary for Wisconsin, OpenStreetMap map tiles, Open-Meteo geocoding, Natural Earth (world-atlas), pyMannKendall, NumPy, SciPy, FastAPI, React, Vite, Plotly.js, Leaflet, Fontsource fonts and Claude Code; the full list is in the repo (package.json, pyproject.toml, docs/sources-checked.md).

This is a NASA Space Apps Challenge project. It is not endorsed by NASA.
